sections.h2: Recording a deed or lien release in person
sections.html:
Documents tied to real estate go to the Harris County Clerk's Real Property Department. It accepts anything a statute authorizes, requires or permits to be filed. The counter is at 201 Caroline, 3rd Floor, Suite 320, open Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The phone number is (713) 274-8680.

Plan to arrive early. Everyone entering the building goes through security, the door to Suite 320 locks promptly at 4:30 p.m., and you need to be inside before 4:00 p.m. if you want a non-certified copy. In a county with more than 3.3 million residents, the clerk may ask for photo identification from anyone filing in person, and each filer shows their own government-issued ID. Bringing a title officer's ID will not cover you.

Releases of lien can also be dropped at the annex offices, but those can take five to seven business days to reach the downtown office. If a closing is on a deadline, file downtown or use e-recording.

Both work, with limits. Mailed originals go to Attn: Real Property Department, P.O. Box 1525, Houston, TX 77251-1525, and the postal service delivers only to that box. A courier with a tracking number uses 201 Caroline, 4th Floor, Suite 460 on weekdays.

Payment by mail has to be a cashier's check, a money order or an approved business or firm check drawn on a U.S. bank. Cash and personal checks are refused. So are temporary checks, estate, trust or association checks, and any check with mark-outs.

E-recording must go through an approved provider, such as Corporation Service Company, eRecording Partners Network or Simplifile. Texas law limits who can e-file to groups like licensed attorneys, banks and credit unions, title insurance companies and agents, state agencies and municipal clerks. A document queued before 2:00 p.m. central time is processed that business day. Anything queued later waits for the next one. As a homeowner you will usually ask your title company or lender to do this for you.

The base charges are short. A deed with a few pages and no more than five names to index sits at the low end of the range.

The records management and archive fees were raised from $6.00 to $10.00. A condominium declaration is recorded at $10.00 per taped sheet, and each key map page attached to a condo filing costs $50. Confirm the current total with the clerk before you write the check.

sections.h2: What the clerk needs on a document
sections.html:
Only original documents or certified copies of court documents get recorded. A photocopy is turned away, and a rejected filing costs you days, so run down this list before you send anything.

  • The signature must be an original and must be notarized, except for an IRS release.
  • Names are printed under every signature, with the capacity of the signer and the entity named.
  • Legal descriptions appear where they apply, along with a printed return address.
  • Leave a margin of 1 to 2 inches across the top and left side for recording information.
  • A conveyance shows each grantee's address, or the filer pays the greater of $25 or twice the recording fee.
  • An abstract of judgment shows the plaintiff's mailing address.

An original will cannot go into the real property records. It belongs with the Probate Department for safekeeping. A probated will can be recorded as a certified copy issued by the probate court, or attached as an exhibit to an affidavit of heirship.

sections.h2: Getting copies and guarding against fraud
sections.html:
The clerk's eCommerce feature sells certified and non-certified copies of recorded documents to the public. Questions about it go to the Public Records Department at 713-274-6390.

The clerk also runs a free Property Alert System. It notifies you when a new real property document is filed under your name. If you rent out a house, have heirs, or suspect a title question, sign up before you list. An unexpected filing is easier to fix before a buyer's title company stumbles on it.

Value and ownership for tax purposes come from the Harris Central Appraisal District at hcad.org, which is a separate office from the clerk. A title company reads the clerk's records for liens, judgments and unresolved heirs. A sale usually pauses until each item is released or paid.

sections.h2: Which recorded papers decide how fast a sale can close?
sections.html:
A title company reads the chain of recorded papers, and each type has its own home in the clerk's files. Gaps show up most often after a death or a missed mortgage payment.

  • After an owner dies, the route depends on the estate: an executor's or administrator's deed for an administered estate, a court order plus the will for a muniment of title, or an affidavit of heirship when neither applies.
  • A transfer on death deed only works if it was recorded before the owner died. The recorded affidavit of death and the death certificate follow it.
  • A foreclosure sale notice must be filed with the clerk and posted at the courthouse at least 21 days before the first-Tuesday auction, which the state sets between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m.
  • A deed of trust is cleared by a recorded release of lien, which the clerk accepts downtown and at the annexes.

A county cannot rewrite an old deed to add heirs, so the fix is always a new recorded instrument. Start the paperwork before you list, because an affidavit or court order can take longer to arrange than the sale itself.

sections.h2: Steps before you list a Harris County house
sections.html:
A short routine saves most closings from delay. First, search the clerk's records under every owner name on the deed and find each deed of trust and its release. Second, sign up for the Property Alert System so a surprise filing reaches you. Third, check with the appraisal district that the owner of record matches the person who will sign. Fourth, if anyone on the chain has died, begin the probate or affidavit work right away. Fifth, gather originals: a photocopy will not be recorded, and the signer's notarized signature is required.

A cash sale skips most of the buyer's lender paperwork, but the title company still records the deed and any lien releases with the clerk. So the same record cleanup applies whether the buyer pays cash or finances.

Harris County is the most populous county in Texas: 5,045,026 people in the July 2025 estimate, up from 4,731,145 at the 2020 census. It counted 2,012,848 housing units, and 30,909 building permits were issued in 2025. Owners live in 54.7 percent of homes. Median home value is $276,600 and median rent is $1,401.

A county this size produces a heavy volume of deeds of trust, liens and affidavits of heirship. That volume is one reason the clerk insists on clean originals, precise fees and approved e-recording vendors.

faqs.q: Where is the Harris County Clerk's real property office?
faqs.a: The in-person counter is at 201 Caroline, 3rd Floor, Suite 320, open Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The phone number is (713) 274-8680.

faqs.q: Does the clerk require a photo ID to file?
faqs.a: Yes, for in-person filing. Texas law lets a clerk in a county of 3.3 million or more require photo identification, and each person shows their own valid government-issued ID.

faqs.q: Can I record a copy of my deed?
faqs.a: No. The clerk takes original documents with original signatures, or certified copies of court documents. A photocopy of a deed is refused.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed?
faqs.a: The posted schedule is $5.00 for the first page, $4.00 for each added page and $0.25 for each name over five, plus a $10.00 archive fee and a $10.00 management fee. Check the clerk's page for the latest amounts.

faqs.q: How do I get alerts when someone files a document under my name?
faqs.a: Sign up for the clerk's free Property Alert System. It notifies you of any new real property document filed under your name.
